idiom_name: module-scope instance + access operation + once-only lazy construction
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the instance exactly one owner — a module or compilation unit, or a class whose construction is closed — and expose one access operation instead of the object itself. Ensure construction runs at most once even under concurrency, using the platform's once-primitive rather than a hand-rolled double-checked test. Where the language already provides module-scope singletons (objects, packages, modules, static type properties, stdlib once-cells), the classic class-plus-static-accessor structure is unnecessary; where a composition root can create the instance and inject it, prefer that and keep the access point for entry points that cannot be injected. The Borg pattern (shared state, many Python instances — see 'related_patterns') is a more flexible alternative that avoids identity coupling. For testing seams, prefer a swappable provider or lazy accessor over reflection-based replacement.
code_sketch:
instance = null                      # owned by the module, not by clients
once    = OncePrimitive()

def get_instance():
    once.run(lambda: set_instance(create_instance()))
    return instance             # created exactly once, lazily
pitfalls: A hand-rolled lazy initialisation (test, lock, test, construct) needs the memory model's blessing; without it another thread can observe a reference to a half-constructed object.

Uniqueness that is only conventional (a public constructor kept in place, a module that can be reloaded) is not uniqueness — in Python, `importlib.reload()` can replace module-level state, making module-level instances not truly process-wide singletons.
Sharing a whole module through one accessor invites unrelated state to accumulate behind a single name.

In Python, module-level state shared across the process is the natural singleton form — a class-based singleton is often unnecessary since `import` already guarantees a single instance of the module object.

Double-checked locking is broken by design on pre-C++11 compilers and pre-Java-5 JVMs; the only correct language-neutral lazy form is the platform's once-primitive (call_once, sync.Once, Lazy<T>, OnceLock, std::once_flag).

In Python, `functools.cache` on an accessor function with parameters caches per argument tuple — the first test's cached value persists for subsequent different arguments unless `cache_clear()` is called between tests.
A frozen dataclass singleton is not immutable: its fields may hold mutable containers (list, dict, set), so appending or mutating them leaks state exactly like any other global.
Import-time side effects (signal handler registration, thread spawning) survive `cache_clear()` of a lazy accessor; clearing the cache creates a second copy of the side effect.

Replacing module-level state via `del module.attribute` does not restore the original — it leaves the module without the name, causing `AttributeError` on re-import rather than reverting to the original.

Wrong move: trust a private constructor to enforce uniqueness -> Java deserialisation mints a fresh instance that bypasses every constructor (pickle/copy can do the same in Python) -> return the canonical object from readResolve, guard clone(), define __reduce__/__getstate__ guards, or close the whole class of bypasses by choosing a form that cannot be reconstructed.

Wrong move: let one singleton's construction reach another singleton's accessor -> circular static/module initialisation can deadlock (each thread holding one class-initialisation lock) or hand back a half-built peer -> declare the dependency instead: inject it, or compose in an explicit init step whose order is written down rather than discovered at runtime.

Wrong move: hand-roll the Java singleton as volatile double-checked locking -> you re-implement guarantees the JVM gives for free while leaving serialisation and reflection bypasses open -> a single-element enum is the canonical Java singleton: deserialised by name via Enum.valueOf (immune to readObject/readResolve) and thread-safe by class initialisation.
sources: Alex Martelli, 'Singleton? We don't need no stinkin' singleton: the Borg design pattern', ActiveState Code, 2001 — introduces the Borg pattern as a shared-state alternative to the GoF Singleton, with Python-specific implementation and critique of identity-focus.

Alex Martelli & David Ascher, 'Avoiding the Singleton Design Pattern with the Borg Idiom', Python Cookbook, 3rd ed. (O'Reilly) — detailed Borg implementation, subclassing behaviour, new-style class compatibility, and comparison with classic Singleton.
Scott Meyers, 'Effective C++', Item 27 — the original Meyers' Singleton (function-local static) and its lazy-initialisation semantics.
Andrei Alexandrescu, 'Modern C++ Design' (2001) — generic Singleton implementations, template policies, and thread-safety analysis pre-C++11.

Microsoft Docs: 'Lazy Initialization' (.NET) — Lazy<T> thread-safety modes (ExecutionAndPublication, PublicationOnly, None), exception caching, and thread-local variant ThreadLocal<T>: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/framework/performance/lazy-initialization.

Rust stdlib docs: OnceLock and LazyLock — thread-safe once primitives for static variables: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.OnceLock.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.LazyLock.html.

C++11 Standard §6.7 [stmt.dcl] p4 — guarantees that local static initialisation is thread-safe: 'If control enters the declaration concurrently while the variable is being initialized, the concurrent execution shall wait for completion of the initialization.'
